name: Preheated blast for iron furnaces
summary: Warming the air blown into an iron furnace saves fuel and raises heat; it is reconstructed at a Han Chinese foundry and was adopted in Scotland in 1829.
description: An incoming air blast is heated before reaching an iron-furnace tuyere. A Han-period cupola is reconstructed with ceramic air ducts recovering heat from the furnace; a later Scottish smelting application used separately heated blast chambers.

evidence.supports: Reconstructs a Han-period Wafangzhuang iron melting furnace with ceramic pipes carrying the blast over the furnace top to preheat it.
Explains that the air route is reconstructed from excavation evidence including heat-exposed pipe surfaces and their inferred orientations.

date.label: By approximately 220 CE
date.basis: The Han-period attribution provides a conservative approximate upper horizon; the specific archaeological operating year is unknown.

events.statement: Archaeological evidence at Wafangzhuang has been reconstructed as Han-period iron-melting cupolas whose incoming blast was heated in pipes passing over the furnace.
events.scope: An archaeologically reconstructed Han iron-melting cupola with ceramic air pipes routed over the hot furnace before entering the lower tuyere.
events.population: Iron-foundry workers at Wafangzhuang in the Han period
events.caveats: The pipes and furnace route are a scholarly reconstruction from fragmentary archaeological remains, not a surviving complete machine or a direct temperature measurement. The period-based approximate latest bound does not locate the first invention; the original excavation publications were not independently inspected. No transfer from Han China to later Scottish practice is claimed.

events.statement: In 1829 heated blast was applied to the main iron-smelting furnace at the Clyde Iron Works, according to the reviewed historical account.
events.scope: An external heated chamber warming the blast before entry to an iron-smelting furnace.
events.caveats: The 1828 foundry trial and application to a main furnace in 1829 are distinct. Early hot-blast claims are disputed; this local witness does not establish worldwide invention or any connection to the Han furnaces.
